confirmed.title: User fn exception swallowed at xFilter cfunc boundary -> silent empty result instead of SQL error
confirmed.claim: When the user's fn (or _tvf_xfilter_impl's NRT allocation) raises, numba's @cfunc boundary swallows the exception, prints to stderr, and returns the int32 zero default. _tvf_xfilter unconditionally returns SQLITE_OK, so the query completes successfully with zero rows: the caller of `SELECT * FROM f(...)` gets a silently-wrong empty result set rather than an error. This triggers on any fn that raises (bad arg, allocation failure inside fn, a bug in fn) and on a NOMEM from structref_meminfo/array materialization inside the njit impl.
confirmed.evidence: _tvf_xfilter has no try/except and returns the constant SQLITE_OK: `def _tvf_xfilter(cur, idx_num, idx_str, argc, argv):` ... `xfilter_impl(cur, argc, argv)` / `return SQLITE_OK` (lines 462-463). The generated _tvf_xfilter_impl (_XFILTER_SRC, lines 110-132) also has no try/except; it calls `result = {fn_call}` (line 125) where {fn_call} is `_fn(...)`. The inline comment (lines 458-461) acknowledges the swallow but asserts 'there is no handle to call sqlite3_result_error'. That is true for sqlite3_result_error, but xFilter signals failure via its OWN return code: a non-SQLITE_OK return from xFilter aborts the SQL statement with an error (every other cfunc here -- xConnect line 168, xOpen line 252, xColumn line 347 -- returns SQLITE_ERROR on `except Exception`). So the error CAN be surfaced; returning SQLITE_OK on failure is the defect.
confirmed.recommendation: Wrap the impl call in a bare try/except inside _tvf_xfilter (NOT try/finally -- numba 0.65.1 RERAISEs on finally) and return SQLITE_ERROR on exception, e.g. `try: xfilter_impl(cur, argc, argv); return SQLITE_OK except Exception: return SQLITE_ERROR`. This both surfaces the error to SQLite and guarantees the cfunc boundary is never crossed by an in-flight exception (matching the catch-only pattern used by the other TVF cfuncs).
confirmed.verify_reasoning: Reading lines 456-463 directly confirms the claim. `_tvf_xfilter` is a `@cfunc` that calls `xfilter_impl(cur, argc, argv)` with no try/except wrapper and unconditionally returns `SQLITE_OK` (line 463). The inline comment at lines 458-461 explicitly acknowledges the swallow, asserting 'there is no handle to call sqlite3_result_error'. That assertion is technically correct for sqlite3_result_error, but the finding's rebuttal is also correct: xFilter signals failure via its own return code, and returning non-SQLITE_OK aborts the SQL statement with an error. Every other cfunc in the file (xConnect line 166, xOpen line 249, xDisconnect line 217, xColumn line 345) wraps its body in `try/except Exception: return SQLITE_ERROR`. The _tvf_xfilter cfunc is the sole exception and is the only one where a user-supplied function is called. The code is structured exactly as the finding describes: `xfilter_impl(cur, argc, argv)` / `return SQLITE_OK` with no exception guard, making user fn exceptions produce silent empty result sets rather than surfaced SQL errors.

confirmed.title: BaseTuple size/offset model ignores alignment padding, disagreeing with numba's padded LLVM tuple layout
confirmed.claim: For BaseTuple types _struct_bytes returns sum(t.bitwidth)//8 (line 96) and _iter_struct_fields assigns offsets by walking fields with no inter-field padding (lines 121-126). numba lowers Tuple/UniTuple/NamedTuple via StructModel.get_value_type -> ir.LiteralStructType([...]) (numba/core/datamodel/models.py:533-537), and an LLVM literal struct is laid out with natural alignment (padding inserted). So the classifier's size and offsets can differ from the layout the call.py codegen actually passes. Concrete trigger: a tuple (int32, double, int32) has bit-packed sum 4+8+4 = 16 -> _classify returns _CLASS_STRUCT_SMALL and the small-struct by-value path in _call_lib_func is taken, but the real LLVM struct {i32, double, i32} aligns the double to offset 8 and totals 24 bytes -> it should be _CLASS_STRUCT_LARGE and passed by pointer/sret. Passing a 24-byte aggregate through the <=16-byte register-coercion path on SysV x86-64 / AAPCS64 is an ABI mismatch: a silent wrong result or stack corruption on that call. The same padding error shifts which eightbyte a float field occupies in _iter_struct_fields, so even within genuinely-16-byte tuples the SSE/INTEGER eightbyte classification (and hence the INT/INT repack decision in _needs_int_int_eightbyte_repack -> _classify_eightbytes) can be wrong; e.g. (int32, double) is modelled as int32@0 + double@4 (cls_lo and cls_hi both SSE), but numba's {i32, double} places the double at offset 8 (lo INTEGER, hi SSE).
confirmed.evidence: abi.py:96 `return sum(t.bitwidth for t in ty.types) // 8`; abi.py:121-126 BaseTuple branch advances `offset += size` with no alignment rounding. The Record branch by contrast uses the dtype's real layout: abi.py:93-94 `ty.size` and abi.py:128-133 `fld.offset`. numba/core/datamodel/models.py:533-537 `StructModel.get_value_type` returns `ir.LiteralStructType([...])` (no `packed=True`), so tuple layout = LLVM natural-alignment layout, which pads. call.py:131/145 use `context.get_value_type(ret_ty)`/`(arg_ty)` (that same padded LiteralStructType) for the alloca/store/by-value coercion, so the 24-byte reality and the 16-byte classifier estimate diverge at the call boundary. test/core/test_abi.py:226-227 even pins this: `_struct_bytes(NamedTuple([int32, int64], MyNT)) == 12`, but `{i32, i64}` is 16 bytes under natural alignment.
confirmed.recommendation: Make the tuple path use the same layout LLVM/numba uses instead of bit-packing. Either compute size/offsets from the target data layout of `context.get_value_type(ty)` (e.g. via the LLVM struct's element offsets / ABI size), or replicate natural-alignment layout in _struct_bytes/_iter_struct_fields (align each field offset up to its size, pad total to max field alignment) so tuples match Records. Add regression cases for (int32, double, int32) [should classify LARGE], (int32, int64) tuple [size 16 not 12], and (int32, double) [eightbytes (INTEGER, SSE) not (SSE, SSE)].
confirmed.verify_reasoning: Verified independently. `abi.py:96` computes `sum(t.bitwidth for t in ty.types) // 8` (bit-packed), while numba lowers `BaseTuple` to `llvmlite.ir.LiteralStructType` with `packed=False`. Confirmed via runtime check: `default_manager.lookup(Tuple([int32, float64, int32])).get_value_type()` returns `{i32, double, i32}` with `packed=False`. Under LLVM natural alignment this struct is 24 bytes (i32@0, double@8, i32@16 + 4B tail padding), but `_struct_bytes` returns 16 (`(32+64+32)//8`), causing `_classify` to return `_CLASS_STRUCT_SMALL` instead of `_CLASS_STRUCT_LARGE`. On SysV x86-64 / AAPCS64, a 24-byte aggregate cannot legally be passed by value in two eightbyte registers; the mismatch causes ABI corruption. The `_iter_struct_fields` docstring at line 115 explicitly documents the bit-packed assumption: 'For `BaseTuple` the fields are bit-packed sequentially with no padding'. A secondary misclassification: `NamedTuple([int32, int64])` gives `_struct_bytes` = 12 but real LLVM size = 16 (`{i32, i64}` with 4B of padding before i64), so `_classify_eightbytes` raises 'expected 16-byte struct' on a type that is actually a valid 16-byte ABI case. Both misclassifications are latent (no current binding uses mixed-width tuple args), but the defect is genuine and the test at `test_abi.py:227` (`_struct_bytes(NamedTuple([int32, int64], MyNT)) == 12`) pins the incorrect behavior rather than the correct one. The `test_call_lib_func_large_return_round_trip_varint_shaped` test uses `_pack_=1` on the ctypes side precisely because `Tuple([intp, uint64, int8])` is classified as LARGE (17 > 16 even bit-packed) and goes via sret pointer; this obscures the bug — it only survives because LARGE path uses a pointer (field offsets agree regardless of padding), not because the size computation is correct.

confirmed.title: get_str_from_p_as_int reads bytes as signed char; non-ASCII C strings raise ValueError instead of decoding
confirmed.claim: The canonical C-string reader interprets each byte through numba's `char` type, which is signed int8 (verified: numba.core.types.char is int8, signed, bitwidth 8). A buffer view is built with `carray(void_p, shape=(MAX_STR_LENGTH,), dtype=char)` and each element is passed to `chr(char_as_code_p)`. For any byte with value 0x80-0xFF the int8 element is negative (-128..-1), and `chr` of a negative value raises `ValueError: chr() arg not in range(0x10ffff)` under njit. So reading any C string that contains a non-ASCII byte (UTF-8 multibyte sequences, Latin-1 high bytes) does not mis-decode quietly -- it throws from inside @njit code. This is the documented canonical primitive used to decode sqlite3_errmsg, file paths, environ values, strerror buffers, and exec error messages; a non-ASCII error message or path therefore turns a normal C-API read into an njit exception.
confirmed.evidence: Line 255-259: `mem_view = carray(void_p, shape=(MAX_STR_LENGTH,), dtype=char)` then `for char_as_code_p in mem_view: if char_as_code_p == 0: return s` and `s += chr(char_as_code_p)`. Import line 9-12 brings `char` from numba.core.types. Confirmed this session via venv python: `numba.core.types.char` reports `int8 signed True bitwidth 8`. Confirmed via njit: `chr(-1)` raises `ValueError: chr() arg not in range(0x10ffff)` and an int8 value cannot even hold 200 (`OverflowError`). The NUL exit `if char_as_code_p == 0` still works (0 is representable), so only bytes >= 0x80 are affected. The only test (test/utils/test_lowlevel.py:165-171) and the round-trip in test/core/test_bindings.py:125 use pure-ASCII strings, so this path is untested.
confirmed.recommendation: Read the buffer through an unsigned byte view so each element is 0..255 before calling chr(). E.g. build the carray with an unsigned 8-bit dtype (numba.core.types.uchar / uint8) instead of `char`, or mask to the low 8 bits (`code & 0xFF`) before `chr`. Note that even with the sign fixed, byte-at-a-time `chr` over a UTF-8 stream produces Latin-1-style per-byte codepoints, not the decoded UTF-8 string; if faithful UTF-8 decoding is intended, the contract/docstring should say it yields raw bytes-as-codepoints, or the bytes should be collected and decoded. At minimum, fix the signedness so high bytes don't raise.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: Read lowlevel.py lines 249-260 directly. Line 10 imports `char` from `numba.core.types`; verified via venv python that `numba.core.types.char` is `int8`, signed=True, bitwidth=8. Line 255: `mem_view = carray(void_p, shape=(MAX_STR_LENGTH,), dtype=char)` builds the view with signed int8 elements. Line 259: `s += chr(char_as_code_p)` — verified that `chr(-1)` and `chr(-128)` raise `ValueError: chr() arg not in range(0x110000)` in CPython. For any byte 0x80-0xFF the int8 element is -128..-1, so `chr` will raise inside the `@njit` body. The NUL exit at line 257 is unaffected (0 is representable as int8). The only test for this function (test/utils/test_lowlevel.py:165-171) uses `'a random string'` — pure ASCII — so the defective path is untested. The finding's reasoning, evidence, and severity are all correct.

confirmed.title: Returned sqlite3* outlives no keep-alive contract; dangles if conn is closed/GC'd
confirmed.claim: extract_connection_ptr returns the raw sqlite3* (db_ptr) as a plain Python int. That pointer is owned by the Python sqlite3.Connection object: it is freed when conn.close() runs or when conn is garbage-collected. The returned int holds no reference to conn, and the docstring's Returns/Raises sections never tell the caller that conn must outlive every use of the pointer. A caller that extracts the pointer, drops its last reference to conn (or calls conn.close()), then passes the int into numbox's @njit bindings gets a use-after-free / segfault on a freed sqlite3* — a silent, hard-to-diagnose crash rather than an exception.
confirmed.evidence: Line 156 `db_ptr = _PysqliteConnection.from_address(id(conn)).db` reads the live handle out of the Connection; line 164 `return db_ptr` hands back only the integer. The docstring Returns block (lines 130-132) says only `int -- sqlite3* as a Python int (intp-compatible)` and the Raises block (lines 134-141) never mentions lifetime. The tests (test/utils/test_pysqlite_bridge.py lines 46-52, 105-113) all keep `conn` alive in a try/finally for the whole pointer-use window, which is exactly the implicit contract that is undocumented — confirming the pointer is only valid while conn lives. CLAUDE.md's own lifetime note (`bind_text/bind_blob ... SQLITE_STATIC ... assumes it outlives the statement`) shows this codebase treats borrowed-pointer ownership as a documented invariant elsewhere.
confirmed.recommendation: Document the keep-alive invariant explicitly in the Returns section: the returned sqlite3* is borrowed from conn and is valid only while conn is alive and open; the caller must retain a reference to conn for the entire lifetime of any @njit use of the pointer, and must not use it after conn.close(). (Cannot bake an actual reference into a bare int, so the contract is the only available mechanism — mirror the SQLITE_STATIC-style ownership note already used for bind_text/bind_blob.)
confirmed.verify_reasoning: Confirmed by direct reading. Line 164 `return db_ptr` hands back a plain Python int with no reference to `conn`. The docstring Returns block (lines 129-132) says only `int -- sqlite3* as a Python int (intp-compatible)` — no lifetime caveat. The Raises block (lines 134-141) covers TypeError and RuntimeError for invalid conn or failed validation, but says nothing about the pointer becoming invalid when conn is closed or GC'd. The tests (lines 46-52, 105-113) keep `conn` alive in try/finally for the entire pointer-use window, which is exactly the implicit contract that is missing from the docs. The CLAUDE.md itself documents lifetime invariants for `bind_text`/`bind_blob` (`SQLITE_STATIC ... assumes it outlives the statement`), confirming the project treats borrowed-pointer ownership as a documented invariant elsewhere. The gap is real.

confirmed.title: xBestIndex bound_mask uses a 64-bit shift that is undefined for n_hidden >= 64
confirmed.claim: bound_mask is a uint64 and the all-bound target is `(uint64(1) << uint64(n_hidden)) - uint64(1)`. A shift of a 64-bit value by >= 64 is undefined at the LLVM level (typically yields 0/poison). For n_hidden == 64 the target accidentally still equals UINT64_MAX (`0 - 1`) and matches a fully-set mask, but for n_hidden >= 65 the per-arg bit `uint64(1) << uint64(h)` for h>=64 also shifts out of range, so a hidden arg can never set its bit and xBestIndex would wrongly reject (or accept) plans. This is unreachable in practice (a TVF with >= 64 hidden scalar args is absurd) but is latent UB in the bitmask logic.
confirmed.evidence: `bound_mask = uint64(0)` (line 192); inside the loop `bound_mask |= uint64(1) << uint64(h)` (line 200); the all-bound check `if bound_mask != (uint64(1) << uint64(n_hidden)) - uint64(1): return SQLITE_CONSTRAINT` (lines 202-203). n_hidden comes from d[0].n_hidden = len(arg_tags), the number of TVF scalar arguments. No upper-bound guard exists on the arg count in _build_tvf_descriptor (lines 384-389 only validate tag kinds).
confirmed.recommendation: Either document/enforce a hidden-arg cap (e.g. raise in _build_tvf_descriptor if len(arg_tags) > 63) or use a count-based all-bound test that avoids the 64-bit shift. Low priority given the input is internal and absurd at that scale.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: Reading lines 192-203 in `_make_xbestindex()` confirms the bitmask logic. `bound_mask = uint64(0)` (line 192), with per-constraint accumulation `bound_mask |= uint64(1) << uint64(h)` (line 200), and the all-bound check `if bound_mask != (uint64(1) << uint64(n_hidden)) - uint64(1)` (line 202). For n_hidden == 64, the shift `uint64(1) << uint64(64)` is undefined at the LLVM level (64-bit shift-by-bit-width is UB; LLVM typically yields 0, making the expression `0 - 1 == UINT64_MAX`, which accidentally works for n_hidden==64). For n_hidden >= 65 the per-arg bit `uint64(1) << uint64(h)` for h>=64 also shifts out of range, so hidden args can never set their bit. `_build_tvf_descriptor` at lines 384-389 validates tag kinds but imposes no upper bound on `len(arg_tags)`. However, the finding correctly assesses this as low severity: a TVF with >= 64 hidden scalar arguments is unreachable in practice.

confirmed.title: _struct_bytes / _iter_struct_fields raise AttributeError on a nested-tuple field instead of a clean TypingError
confirmed.claim: The BaseTuple branches assume every field exposes `.bitwidth` (line 96 and lines 123). A BaseTuple containing a nested struct-shaped field (e.g. a Tuple of Tuples or Tuple of Record) has a field with no `.bitwidth`, so `sum(t.bitwidth ...)` / `ft.bitwidth // 8` raises a raw AttributeError rather than the clean, caller-naming TypingError the surrounding code goes out of its way to emit (lines 97-100, 135-138) for the not-struct-shaped case. Low impact: nested-aggregate tuple signatures are not currently a supported binding shape, so this is robustness, not a live failure.
confirmed.evidence: abi.py:96 `sum(t.bitwidth for t in ty.types)` and abi.py:123 `size = ft.bitwidth // 8` both dereference `.bitwidth` unconditionally on each tuple element; nothing restricts the element type to a scalar. The intent to surface clean errors is explicit in abi.py:97-100 and abi.py:135-138.
confirmed.recommendation: If hardening is desired, guard the tuple-element loop to raise the same TypingError (naming the caller) when a field lacks `.bitwidth` / is itself struct-shaped; otherwise document that tuple bindings must be flat scalar tuples.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: Verified directly in source. `abi.py:96` calls `t.bitwidth` unconditionally for every element in `ty.types`. `abi.py:123` calls `ft.bitwidth // 8` unconditionally. A `BaseTuple` element that is itself a `BaseTuple` or `Record` has no `.bitwidth` attribute, so both lines raise a raw `AttributeError`. The surrounding code explicitly goes out of its way to emit clean `TypingError` messages (lines 97-100 for the outer type, lines 135-138 for `_iter_struct_fields`), making the gap in the inner guard inconsistent. The finding correctly notes this is a robustness issue (low severity) since nested-aggregate tuple bindings are not a currently supported shape, but the inconsistency is genuine.

confirmed.title: get_str_from_p_as_int crashes on non-ASCII C strings (signed char -> chr() out of range)
confirmed.claim: get_str_from_p_as_int reads the C string with dtype=char, which numba defines as signed int8. Any byte >= 0x80 (every continuation/lead byte of a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence) reads back as a negative value (e.g. 0xC3 -> -61). The loop then calls chr(char_as_code_p) on that negative value, which raises ValueError: chr() arg not in range(0x10ffff). So instead of returning the string, the function raises on any C string containing a non-ASCII byte. This is the documented canonical reader for NUL-terminated C strings, and CLAUDE.md directs callers to decode sqlite3_errmsg (UTF-8, may contain non-ASCII from table/column names) via this exact function; such an error message read would crash the caller.
confirmed.evidence: Lines 255-259: `mem_view = carray(void_p, shape=(MAX_STR_LENGTH,), dtype=char)` then `for char_as_code_p in mem_view: if char_as_code_p == 0: return s; s += chr(char_as_code_p)`. `char` is imported from numba.core.types (line 11) and is int8/signed (verified this session: `numba.core.types.char` repr is `int8`, `.signed` is True). Reproduced this session: calling get_str_from_p_as_int on a buffer holding the UTF-8 bytes 0xC3 0xA9 0x41 0x00 ('eA') raised `ValueError: chr() arg not in range(0x10ffff)`. The NUL check (`== 0`) is unaffected because only 0x00 is zero, but every byte in 0x80..0xFF is negative under int8 and triggers the chr() failure.
confirmed.recommendation: Read bytes as unsigned (use an unsigned 8-bit dtype, e.g. numba.core.types.uint8, for the carray view) so byte values land in 0..255 before chr(). Note that even unsigned, byte-wise chr() still mis-decodes multi-byte UTF-8 (each byte becomes its own codepoint); for correct text the bytes should be collected and UTF-8-decoded. At minimum switch to the unsigned dtype to stop the crash; preferably accumulate raw bytes and decode as UTF-8 to match the 'copying the original string's data' contract on the line-251 docstring.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: Line 10 imports `char` from `numba.core.types`; verified at runtime that `numba.core.types.char` has repr `int8` and `.signed == True`. Line 255: `mem_view = carray(void_p, shape=(MAX_STR_LENGTH,), dtype=char)` — so each element is a signed int8. Line 259: `s += chr(char_as_code_p)` — any byte in 0x80..0xFF reads back as a negative value (e.g. 0xC3 -> -61), and `chr(-61)` raises `ValueError: chr() arg not in range(0x110000)` (confirmed by direct Python evaluation). The NUL-terminator check `== 0` on line 257 is unaffected since only 0x00 is zero; every continuation byte of a UTF-8 multi-byte sequence triggers the crash path. The finding's claim is accurate: the function is documented in CLAUDE.md as the canonical C-string reader (including for `sqlite3_errmsg`), making this a real correctness defect for any non-ASCII string data.

confirmed.title: No format-spec / argument cross-validation in @njit path: spec-vs-type or spec-vs-count mismatch silently miscompiles where pure-Python raises
confirmed.claim: The @njit codegen layer validates each arg is a printf-able scalar (_validate_writer_arg_type) but never cross-checks the argument types/count against the conversion specifiers in the literal format string. A type mismatch such as printf("%d\n", 3.5) is accepted: the float64 is passed through in an SSE register while libc reads a GP integer register for %d, returning a silent wrong result. A count mismatch such as printf("%d %d\n", 5) reads an undefined varargs slot (garbage / crash). In pure-Python mode the very same calls raise cleanly (Python's % raises TypeError 'not enough arguments for format string' / '%d format: a number is required, not float'), so the two modes diverge: one errors, the other miscompiles. Triggers whenever a caller's specifiers don't line up with the supplied args by type or count in @njit.
confirmed.evidence: _validate_writer_arg_type (line 210-227) only checks `isinstance(unliteral(ty), (Float, Integer, Boolean, UnicodeType))` per-arg — it has the literal fmt_str available in the intrinsic (extract_literal_str at e.g. line 312) but never parses its specifiers nor compares specifier count to len(args_ty). _emit_variadic_call (line 271-301) promotes args via _promote_for_varargs and emits `builder.call(fn, ...)` with `var_arg=True` (line 299) — no specifier-driven typing. By contrast the pure-Python wrappers (e.g. printf line 537: `text = _python_fmt_compat(fmt) % args`) let Python's % operator enforce spec/arg agreement and raise on mismatch. The %n regex already parses specifiers, so a specifier walk is feasible here.
confirmed.recommendation: At typing time, scan the literal format string for conversion specifiers (reuse/extend the existing specifier regex) and verify (a) the specifier count equals len(args_ty) and (b) each specifier's expected class (integer d/i/o/u/x/X/c, float e/f/g/a, string s, pointer p) matches the corresponding arg type — raising TypingError on mismatch. This restores cross-mode parity (Python already raises) and closes the silent-wrong-result / undefined-varargs-read window. If full type matching is deemed too strict, at minimum enforce the specifier-count check, which is unambiguous and catches the crash-prone under-supply case.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: Verified against the live source. `_validate_writer_arg_type` at lines 210-227 only checks `isinstance(unliteral(ty), (Float, Integer, Boolean, UnicodeType))` per arg — no specifier parsing. `_emit_variadic_call` at lines 271-301 promotes args via `_promote_for_varargs` and emits `builder.call(fn, ..., var_arg=True)` at line 299 with no specifier-driven cross-check. The literal format string IS available at typing time (`extract_literal_str` at line 312); it is simply never parsed for specifier count or class matching. A float64 passed for `%d` goes into an SSE register while libc reads a GP register — silent wrong result. An under-supplied args tuple leaves a varargs slot uninitialized — silent garbage or crash. By contrast, the pure-Python path at line 537 (`_python_fmt_compat(fmt) % args`) lets Python's `%` operator enforce both type and count, raising `TypeError` on mismatch. The `%n` checker in the same file already walks the format string for rejection, confirming a specifier walk is feasible. The two-mode divergence (one raises, one silently miscompiles) is real.

confirmed.title: A raising user fn yields a silently-successful empty result set, indistinguishable from a legitimately-empty TVF
confirmed.claim: When the user's fn raises inside xfilter_impl, the @cfunc boundary of _tvf_xfilter swallows the exception and returns the zero default (0 == SQLITE_OK). Because _tvf_xfilter_impl zeroes the cursor's mi_p/data_p/n_rows/row_stride at the top (lines 114-119) BEFORE calling _fn (line 125), a raise leaves the cursor empty, so _tvf_xeof returns 1 immediately and SQLite reports a successful query that returns zero rows. The caller cannot distinguish a fn that errored from a fn that legitimately produced an empty array -- a silent wrong result (no error surfaced, no rows).
confirmed.evidence: The cfunc comment itself states the behavior: "If the user fn raises inside xfilter_impl, the @cfunc boundary swallows the exception and returns the zero default (SQLITE_OK), so SQLite sees a successful query with no rows rather than an error. Unlike a UDF, xFilter gets no sqlite3_context, so there is no handle to call sqlite3_result_error." (lines 458-461). Body: `xfilter_impl(cur, argc, argv); return SQLITE_OK` (lines 462-463). The top-of-impl reset (`if c[0].mi_p != 0: release_meminfo(...); c[0].mi_p = 0; c[0].data_p = 0; c[0].n_rows = 0; ...`, lines 114-119) runs before `result = {fn_call}` (line 125), and the only raising operation is `_fn(...)`; the subsequent field stores (mi_p/data_p/n_rows/row_stride, lines 128-132) do not raise -- so the failure mode is exactly 'empty result', never garbage rows. _tvf_xeof (lines 276-281) returns 1 when `data_p == 0`. This matches the documented reference note that a numba @cfunc swallows exceptions and returns the zero default with no unwind to C.
confirmed.recommendation: Surface the error rather than swallowing it silently. xFilter cannot call sqlite3_result_error (no sqlite3_context), but it CAN store an error string on the vtab's zErrMsg (sqlite3_vtab.zErrMsg, freed by SQLite) and return a non-zero rc from _tvf_xfilter, which SQLite propagates as a query error. Wrap xfilter_impl in a bare try/except inside the cfunc (per the documented exception-curing pattern), set zErrMsg via sqlite3_malloc/sqlite3_mprintf, and return SQLITE_ERROR; at minimum document the limitation in register_tvf's docstring (it currently documents only the unbound-arg rejection and NaN->NULL, not the swallowed-fn-error case).
confirmed.verify_reasoning: The @cfunc at lines 456-463 is confirmed to call `xfilter_impl(cur, argc, argv)` and then unconditionally `return SQLITE_OK`. The generated template (_XFILTER_SRC, lines 113-131) zeroes the cursor fields mi_p/data_p/n_rows/row_stride (lines 114-119) BEFORE `result = {fn_call}` (line 125). A raise at line 125 leaves data_p == 0. _tvf_xeof (lines 276-281) returns 1 when `c[0].data_p == 0 or c[0].rowid >= c[0].n_rows`, so SQLite sees an immediately-exhausted cursor. The cfunc comment itself states: "If the user fn raises inside xfilter_impl, the @cfunc boundary swallows the exception and returns the zero default (SQLITE_OK), so SQLite sees a successful query with no rows rather than an error." (lines 458-461). The finding is genuine: a raising fn and a legitimately-empty fn are indistinguishable to the caller.

confirmed.title: BaseTuple size/offset model omits alignment padding, diverging from numba's actual LLVM StructModel layout
confirmed.claim: _struct_bytes and _iter_struct_fields compute the size and field offsets of a BaseTuple as a bit-packed sequence with no inter-field padding. numba lowers a Tuple to a non-packed LLVM LiteralStructType via StructModel, and call.py's codegen uses exactly that lowering (context.get_value_type(arg_ty)). For a tuple with mixed-width fields the two layouts disagree: e.g. Tuple((int32, int64)) is modeled here as 12 bytes with the int64 at offset 4, but the LLVM value type {i32, i64} that is actually passed/returned is 16 bytes with the int64 at offset 8. Because the abi.py size feeds (a) the SMALL/LARGE classification threshold (_classify, line 80) and (b) the exactly-16-byte gate of _needs_int_int_eightbyte_repack (call.py:227), a tuple that is really 16 bytes in LLVM but computed as < 16 here is never repacked. That is the very INT/INT field-dropping hazard the repack path exists to fix (call.py:212-233), so on SysV-x86-64 / AAPCS64 such a by-value tuple arg or return can silently drop a field and produce a wrong result.

So a tuple whose true LLVM size is 16 but whose packed size is < 16 bypasses the repack. The Record branch is unaffected — Record carries real C offsets (abi.py:128-133 use fld.offset) and ty.size (abi.py:94), which already account for padding.
confirmed.recommendation: Derive tuple field offsets and total size from numba's actual data model rather than a hand-rolled bit-pack — e.g. query the StructModel / LLVM struct layout used by call.py's get_value_type so abi.py and codegen agree, applying each field's natural alignment and the trailing pad to a multiple of the max field alignment. At minimum, restrict supported tuple signatures to uniform-width or canonical {i64,i64} shapes and reject mixed-width tuples with a clear TypingError until the aligned layout is implemented.
confirmed.verify_reasoning: abi.py:95-96 `return sum(t.bitwidth for t in ty.types) // 8` is a pure bit-pack. For Tuple((int32, int64)), this yields (32+64)//8 = 12. The repack that would prevent llvmlite from dropping the second eightbyte's field is therefore skipped for such tuples. The same divergence affects _classify_eightbytes (called only when _struct_bytes == 16, so it would never be reached for the 12-byte mismatch case). The defect is latent: signatures.py line 6 shows `lldiv_t = Tuple((int64, int64))` as the only Tuple return type in the shipped signatures, and Tuple((int64,int64)) is unaffected (both fields are 64-bit, no padding; _is_canonical_int64_pair_layout returns True and skips repack correctly). The finding's reasoning holds exactly. Severity adjusted to medium because the defect is latent — no shipped signature triggers it.

For such a function prepend = max(0, co_firstlineno - 13) = 0, so the wrapper's @njit is compiled at file line 13 instead of at the real decorator line. confirmed.title: QUAL_SEP='.' qualified-name parsing via rsplit('.',1) mis-parses any source or variable name containing a dot

confirmed.title: Explicit End/Derived `ty` not included in the kernel fingerprint

confirmed.title: get_input bounds check ignores negative indices
confirmed.claim: ol_get_input only validates the upper bound. A negative i (e.g. get_input(-1)) passes num_inputs and the check `if i >= num_inputs` is False, so `self.inputs[i]` is evaluated with a negative index. numba's typed List applies Python-style negative indexing, so get_input(-1) silently returns the LAST input instead of raising the intended out-of-range NumbaError. The caller asked for input -1 (an invalid id) and gets a wrong node back rather than an error.
confirmed.evidence: Lines 83-87: `def _(self, i): num_inputs = len(self.inputs); if i >= num_inputs: raise NumbaError(...); return self.inputs[i]`. The guard is one-sided. The Python wrapper get_input at line 22-23 (`return cast(self._get_input(i), typeof(self))`) and the njit _get_input at line 25-27 pass i through unchecked, so any negative i reaches `self.inputs[i]`. numba typed List indexing mirrors Python list semantics (negative index = from-end), making get_input(-1) return inputs[num_inputs-1] silently. A large negative (i < -num_inputs) would instead raise an IndexError from the List, so the error message is inconsistent with the i>=num_inputs path.
confirmed.recommendation: Change the guard to `if i < 0 or i >= num_inputs:` so the existing NumbaError message covers the full invalid range, matching the index contract the message implies ("Requested input {i} while the node has {num_inputs} inputs").

A negative `i` satisfies `i >= num_inputs` as False (e.g. -1 >= 5 is False), so execution proceeds to `return self.inputs[i]` at line 87. numba's typed List mirrors Python list semantics for negative indices, so `self.inputs[-1]` silently returns the last element. The intended error message at line 86 ('Requested input {i} while the node has {num_inputs} inputs') implies a full range contract, making the omission a real behavioral gap. The finding's reasoning holds exactly as stated.

confirmed.title: Method param assertion rejects legitimate defaults whose repr() differs from source spelling
confirmed.claim: make_structref(..., struct_methods=...) raises AssertionError for an otherwise-valid method whenever a parameter default's source spelling differs from repr(default). Examples that fail: `def m(self, n=1_000)` (source `1_000` vs repr `1000`), `def m(self, n=0x10)` (source `0x10` vs repr `16`), `def m(self, s="a, b")` (double-quoted source vs single-quoted repr). confirmed.title: Header regex [^)]* cannot match a method signature containing ')' in a default or annotation
confirmed.claim: The header-extraction regex captures the parameter list with `([^)]*)`, which stops at the FIRST ')'. A legitimate method whose signature contains a nested ')' — e.g. `def m(self, x=factory())` or `def m(self, f: Callable[[int], int])` — is mis-captured (truncated at the inner ')'), so the subsequent `assert params_str == params_str_` fails (or, combined with the count check, `assert len(method_header) == 1` can mis-count). The canonical pattern already exists at line 252.

For input `"%%ld"`, the regex matches starting at position 1 (the second `%`): the sequence `%ld` satisfies the pattern (empty flags/width, `l` as length modifier, `d` as conversion). confirmed.title: uint64 bound_mask in xBestIndex is undefined / wrong for a TVF with 64 or more hidden args

The name describes loading an array row INTO a dict, but this overload registers `_load_dict_into_array` and emits `_load_to_array_(array_, sheaf_)` which does the opposite: it copies sheaf (dict) values INTO the array (`array_[0].{field} = sheaf_[...].get_as(...)`). The name is a verbatim copy of the genuinely-named overload in loader_utils.py:33 (`ol_load_array_row_into_dict`, which really does load an array row into a dict). A future maintainer grepping `ol_load_array_row_into_dict` gets two hits with opposite semantics; the misnamed one will mislead.

The combine_utils stub it registers is named `_load_dict_into_array` (combine_utils.py:36), confirming the intended direction is dict->array, so the `ol_load_array_row_into_dict` name is wrong for that module.

Purely local; the overload function's identifier is never referenced elsewhere (numba keys off the @overload target `_load_dict_into_array`, not the function name), so the rename is zero-risk.
